paragraphs.heading: What counts as a fossil
paragraphs.text: A fossil is anything left behind by a living thing from a past geological age: its preserved remains, an impression of it, or some other trace. The word comes from a Latin term meaning 'obtained by digging'. Bones, shells, petrified wood, hair and objects preserved in amber all qualify, and so do leftover bits of DNA. A specimen is sometimes counted as a fossil once it is more than 10,000 years old.

paragraphs.heading: Bodies, traces and chemicals
paragraphs.text: A fossil usually keeps only part of the dead organism. Most often it is a part that already held minerals during life, such as bones and teeth. Other fossils are not body parts at all. They are marks an organism made while it was alive, such as animal tracks or droppings, and these are called trace fossils to set them apart from body fossils. A further kind is biochemical, and these are known as chemofossils.

paragraphs.heading: From microbes to giant trees
paragraphs.text: Fossils come in a huge range of sizes. The smallest are bacteria one micrometre across. At the other end are dinosaurs and trees many metres long that weigh many tons. The largest fossil known so far is a Sequoia at Coaldale, Nevada, which measures 88 m in length. The oldest fossils are around 3.48 billion to 4.1 billion years old.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the fossil record
paragraphs.text: All fossils taken together are called the fossil record. It is incomplete, yet many studies have shown that it holds enough information to give a good picture of how life on Earth diversified. In the 19th century people noticed that certain fossils went with certain layers of rock. That led to a geological timescale and to knowing the relative ages of different fossils. In the early 20th century, radiometric dating let scientists measure the absolute ages of rocks and of the fossils inside them. The study of fossils, including their age, how they formed and what they mean for evolution, is part of paleontology.

paragraphs.heading: Fossils as treasures and charms
paragraphs.text: Documented human dealings with fossils go back as far as recorded history, or earlier. Many Paleolithic stone knives found in Europe have a fossil echinoderm set exactly at the hand grip, and they date back to Homo heidelbergensis and the Neanderthals. The ancient Egyptians collected fossils that looked like the bones of modern species they worshipped. Their god Set was linked with the hippopotamus, so fossil bones of hippo-like species were kept in his temples.

paragraphs.heading: Tongue stones and dragon bones
paragraphs.text: Fossils appear to have fed directly into the myths of many civilizations. The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder wrote about "tongue stones". These were fossil shark teeth, which some classical cultures thought looked like the tongues of people or snakes. In Japan, fossil shark teeth were taken for the razor-sharp claws of a mythical creature, the tengu. In medieval China, fossil bones of ancient mammals were often taken to be "dragon bones" and were used as medicine.

paragraphs.heading: Early explanations
paragraphs.text: The Greek scholar Aristotle eventually came to see that fossil seashells in rocks resembled shells found on the beach, which indicated that the fossils had once been living animals. In his Dream Pool Essays, published in 1088, the Chinese scholar-official Shen Kuo considered marine fossils found in a rock layer of mountains hundreds of miles from the Pacific Ocean. He proposed that they showed a prehistoric seashore had once been there and had moved over centuries of time.
